opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing is that it just gets out of the way. When you're pair programming, the worst thing is when the tool itself becomes friction: lag, blurry screen sharing, fighting over who has control. With Tuple, the screen sharing is really crisp and low-latency, so it actually feels like you're sitting next to someone looking at the same monitor.

The other big thing is that both people can drive. You can each have your own cursor and take control of the other person's machine pretty seamlessly. So if I'm watching someone work and I want to point at something or quickly type out an idea, I don't have to say "okay, go to line 142, no, scroll up a bit." I can just do it. That makes pairing much more fluid, a real back-and-forth rather than one person typing while the other narrates.

I've found pair programming is really valuable, especially when you're onboarding someone or working through a tricky bug. You pick up a lot of tacit knowledge from watching how someone else works: their shortcuts, how they debug, what they check first. Tuple makes that cheap enough that you actually do it, instead of it feeling like a big scheduled event. You can just hop on for fifteen minutes with someone, and that low barrier ends up mattering a lot.

r001.rationale: The response describes both people taking control and contributing during pairing, but it does not characterize the work as one person doing it while the other reviews in real time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so pair programming is something I do a lot at Anthropic, and I think it's honestly one of the most underrated ways to work. And Tuple is the tool we've mostly settled on for doing it remotely.

The thing I like most is that it's really low friction. It's basically built for exactly one purpose, which is two people looking at the same screen and both being able to type. So you call someone, you're in, you can see their editor, and either of you can grab the keyboard whenever. There's no "let me share my screen, okay can you see it, oh it's blurry" dance that you get with Zoom or Meet. The latency is low enough that it actually feels like you're sitting next to the person, which matters a lot more than you'd think. If there's a half-second lag every time you move the cursor, people stop driving and just start dictating, and then you lose a lot of the benefit.

I also think the fact that both people can control the screen changes the dynamic. With regular screen sharing it's very much "one person works, one person watches," and the watcher tends to check out. With Tuple it's more like you're genuinely both working on it. Someone can just reach in and fix a typo, or pull up a file to point at something, without having to narrate it.

And then there's a bunch of the stuff that pair programming is good for in general, which Tuple just makes easier to actually do. It's great for onboarding, where someone new can watch how an experienced person navigates the codebase and all the little tricks they use. It's great when you're stuck, because you've got someone there to notice the thing you've been staring past for twenty minutes. And it keeps you honest. It's a lot harder to get distracted or go down some rabbit hole when there's another person watching.

So I'd say the thing I like about Tuple specifically is just that it gets out of the way. The point is the pairing, and it's the tool that's made remote pairing feel closest to the in-person version.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts screen sharing, where one person works and the other watches, with Tuple enabling both people to work. It does not describe the second person as reviewing the work in real time.
